title: Golf Anatomy (2nd Edition)
author: Craig Davies and Vince DiSaia
summary:
"Golf Anatomy" is a reference-style fitness manual, not a narrative book, built around a single premise: that most amateur golfers' swing faults, inconsistency, and injuries are downstream of physical limitations — restricted mobility, poor stability, weak rotational strength — rather than pure technique flaws. Written by chiropractor and golf performance specialist Craig Davies and strength-and-conditioning specialist Vince DiSaia, the book pairs full-color anatomical illustrations with 72 targeted exercises, organized to build a golfer's body systematically from mobility through explosive power.

The book opens by establishing the golf swing itself as an athletic movement with specific physical demands — rotational range of motion through the hips, thoracic spine, and shoulders, combined with the ability to stabilize the lower body while the upper body rotates rapidly. The authors argue that most golf instruction focuses exclusively on swing mechanics and club-fitting while ignoring whether a golfer's body is even physically capable of executing the positions being taught, leading to compensations that both reduce performance and create injury risk over time.

From there, the book proceeds through a deliberately sequenced training progression rather than a random exercise catalog. It begins with a structured pre-round warm-up designed to prepare the body for the specific demands of a swing, then moves into mobility work targeting the joints most commonly restricted in golfers — hips, thoracic spine, shoulders — before addressing balance and proprioception, the body's ability to sense and control its position during the dynamic, asymmetric loading of a swing.

The middle-to-late chapters build toward performance: rotational resistance and deceleration training aimed specifically at reducing the injury risk created by the repeated, forceful rotation and abrupt stop inherent to a golf swing, followed by strength training for distance and explosive power training aimed at increasing clubhead speed. Each exercise is presented with anatomical illustrations showing the specific muscles engaged, allowing a reader to understand not just how to perform a movement but why it targets a particular swing-relevant physical quality.

The book closes with a program-planning chapter that ties the preceding exercise chapters together into structured, sequenced training plans, addressing how to combine mobility, stability, strength, and power work across a training week or season, and how to adjust programming based on a golfer's specific physical limitations, playing frequency, and goals — moving the reader from a menu of individual exercises to an actual, sustainable fitness program built around their own game.

sections.title: The Golfer in Motion
sections.summary:
This opening chapter establishes the biomechanical foundation for the rest of the book: what the golf swing actually demands of the body. It opens by breaking the swing into its component phases and identifying the specific ranges of motion, forces, and muscle groups involved at each stage.

The chapter's substance walks through the swing as an athletic sequence — the backswing's demand for hip and shoulder rotation, the transition's demand for stored elastic energy and stability, and the downswing and follow-through's demand for explosive rotational power and deceleration control — framing each phase in terms of the specific physical capacities a golfer's body needs to execute it without compensation or injury.

The chapter closes by making the case, central to the whole book, that swing faults commonly attributed purely to technique are frequently downstream of physical limitations, setting up the following chapters' progression through warm-up, mobility, and stability training as the physical foundation technique instruction alone cannot substitute for.
keyLessons: The golf swing places specific, identifiable demands on hip, thoracic spine, and shoulder mobility that vary by swing phase.
Many swing faults attributed to technique are actually downstream effects of physical limitations.
Effective golf fitness training should be sequenced to match the biomechanical demands of each swing phase.

sections.title: Preworkout Warm-Up
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses the specific warm-up needed before either a training session or a round of golf, distinct from general athletic warm-ups. It opens by noting that many golfers either skip warm-up entirely or use generic static stretching poorly matched to the swing's actual demands.

The chapter provides a sequence of dynamic warm-up exercises designed to raise tissue temperature and activate the specific muscle groups and movement patterns used in a swing, priming the body for the rotational, asymmetric loading that follows.

It closes by linking proper warm-up to injury prevention and consistency, arguing that a golfer who arrives at the first tee under-prepared physically is more likely to compensate technically, undermining performance from the very first swing.
keyLessons: Generic static stretching is a poor substitute for a warm-up matched to the swing's actual movement demands.
Dynamic, swing-specific warm-up exercises prepare the exact muscle groups and ranges of motion used in play.
Under-preparing physically before play increases the likelihood of technical compensation and injury.

sections.title: Mobility for Optimal Swing Angles
sections.summary:
This chapter targets the specific joints most commonly restricted in golfers — hips, thoracic spine, and shoulders — and their direct effect on swing positions. It opens by explaining how restricted mobility in these areas forces compensatory movement elsewhere in the swing, often in the lower back, which bears the resulting strain.

The chapter's substance presents targeted mobility exercises for each restricted area, explaining the specific swing angle or position each exercise is designed to unlock, paired with anatomical illustrations of the muscles and joints involved.

It closes by connecting improved mobility to the following chapter's focus on balance, arguing that increased range of motion is only useful for performance if the golfer can also control and stabilize that range under the dynamic load of an actual swing.
keyLessons: Restricted hip, thoracic spine, or shoulder mobility commonly forces compensatory strain onto the lower back during a swing.
Mobility exercises should be selected based on which specific swing angle or position they are intended to unlock.
Increased mobility alone is insufficient without the stability to control the new range of motion.

sections.title: Balance and Proprioception Training for Efficient Energy Transfer
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses the body's ability to sense and control its position, particularly under the asymmetric, rotational loading of a golf swing. It opens by describing how poor balance and body awareness cause energy leaks during the swing, reducing both power and consistency even when mobility and strength are adequate.

The chapter's substance presents exercises designed to train proprioception and balance under conditions that mimic the dynamic instability of an actual swing, rather than static balance drills disconnected from the sport's actual movement pattern.

It closes by framing efficient energy transfer — the ability to move force smoothly from the ground through the body into the clubhead — as depending on this trained balance and body awareness, setting up the following chapter's focus on controlling and decelerating that transferred force safely.
keyLessons: Poor balance and body awareness cause energy leaks during the swing that reduce power even when other physical qualities are adequate.
Balance training for golf should mimic the dynamic, asymmetric instability of an actual swing rather than static balance alone.
Efficient transfer of force from the ground through the body depends on trained proprioception, not strength alone.

sections.title: Rotational Resistance and Deceleration for Injury-Free Swings
sections.summary:
This chapter focuses on the injury-prevention side of the swing's repeated forceful rotation and abrupt stop, an area the authors argue is commonly neglected in golf fitness training that focuses only on generating power. It opens by explaining the injury mechanism: the body must not only produce rotational force but also safely absorb and stop that same force at the end of the swing, repeatedly, often thousands of times per season.

The chapter's substance presents resistance-based training exercises specifically targeting the muscles responsible for controlling and decelerating rotation, aimed at building the tissue resilience needed to withstand this repeated deceleration without injury.

It closes by connecting deceleration control to the following chapters' focus on strength and power, arguing that a golfer should not add power training on top of an unprepared deceleration system, since doing so increases injury risk rather than simply increasing distance.
keyLessons: The golf swing requires the body to safely decelerate the same rotational force it generates, repeatedly, over a season.
Training focused only on generating power while neglecting deceleration control increases injury risk.
Rotational resistance training builds the tissue resilience needed to handle repeated forceful stops.

sections.title: Strength for Increased Distance
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses general strength development as a foundation for distance, distinct from the more specialized power training that follows. It opens by explaining how baseline strength in the major muscle groups involved in the swing supports both distance and the ability to maintain form over a full round or season.

The chapter's substance presents strength-building exercises targeting the core, hips, and upper body, explaining how each contributes to the kinetic chain that ultimately determines clubhead speed.

It closes by distinguishing general strength from the following chapter's explosive power, framing strength as the necessary foundation that power training builds on top of, rather than a substitute for it.
keyLessons: Baseline strength in the core, hips, and upper body supports both distance and the ability to maintain form over a full round.
Strength exercises should be selected based on their contribution to the swing's kinetic chain, not general fitness alone.
General strength training is a foundation for, rather than a substitute for, more specialized power training.

sections.title: Explosive Power for Longer Drives
sections.summary:
This chapter moves from baseline strength into power — the rate at which force can be generated — as the specific physical quality most directly tied to clubhead speed and driving distance. It opens by distinguishing power from raw strength, noting that a golfer can be strong without being able to apply that strength quickly enough to matter for swing speed.

The chapter's substance presents explosive, often plyometric-style exercises designed to train the nervous system and muscles to generate force rapidly, mirroring the very short window of time available during the downswing to transfer force into the club.

It closes by cautioning that power training should be layered onto an already-established foundation of mobility, stability, and deceleration control from earlier chapters, rather than attempted first, given its higher injury risk if the underlying physical qualities aren't yet in place.
keyLessons: Power (the rate of force production) is distinct from raw strength and is more directly tied to clubhead speed.
Explosive, plyometric-style training targets the nervous system's ability to generate force within the short time window of a downswing.
Power training carries higher injury risk and should be layered onto an established foundation of mobility and deceleration control, not attempted first.

sections.title: Program Planning
sections.summary:
This closing chapter ties the preceding exercise-focused chapters into structured, sequenced training programs. It opens by acknowledging that a menu of individual exercises is of limited use without a plan for how to combine and sequence them across a training week or season.

The chapter's substance provides guidance on structuring training blocks — sequencing mobility, stability, strength, and power work appropriately, adjusting for a golfer's specific physical limitations identified in earlier chapters, and accounting for playing frequency and goals (distance versus consistency versus injury recovery, for instance).

The chapter, and the book, closes by positioning program planning as the step that turns the book from a reference catalog into an actual usable fitness system, encouraging readers to revisit earlier chapters' assessments to build a program suited to their specific physical starting point rather than following a generic template.
keyLessons: Individual exercises have limited value without a program that sequences them appropriately across a training period.
Training programs should be built around a golfer's specific physical limitations and goals, not a generic template.
Program structure should progress through mobility, stability, strength, and power in a deliberate order rather than randomly.
Many golf swing faults commonly blamed on technique are actually downstream effects of physical limitations in mobility, stability, or strength.
A proper pre-round warm-up should be dynamic and swing-specific, not generic static stretching.
Restricted hip and thoracic spine mobility commonly forces compensatory, injury-prone strain onto the lower back.
Balance and proprioception training should mimic the dynamic instability of an actual swing to improve energy transfer.
The body must be trained to safely decelerate rotational force, not just generate it, to avoid injury from repeated swings.
General strength is a necessary foundation that should be established before adding higher-risk explosive power training.
Power (rate of force production) is distinct from raw strength and is the physical quality most directly tied to clubhead speed.
An individualized, sequenced training program built around a specific golfer's limitations outperforms following a generic exercise list.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Kinetic Chain
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The sequenced transfer of force from the ground, through the legs, hips, and torso, and finally into the arms and clubhead during a golf swing; the book frames nearly every exercise category (mobility, stability, strength, power) as targeting a specific link in this chain, since a weak or restricted link anywhere reduces overall efficiency and increases compensation elsewhere.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Golf's Five Problem Areas (Injury Zones)
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A framework, referenced across the book's injury-prevention material, identifying the body regions most commonly injured by the repetitive, asymmetric demands of the golf swing — generally including the lower back, shoulders, wrists/hands, hips, and knees — used to target mobility and resistance training toward the areas at greatest risk.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Rotational Resistance and Deceleration for Injury-Free Swings

actionSteps: Before your next round, replace static stretching with five minutes of dynamic warm-up movements that mimic the actual rotational pattern of a swing.
Pick the single body region (hips, thoracic spine, or shoulders) where you notice the most restriction in your own swing and commit to two mobility exercises for that region, three times this week.
Add one balance or single-leg stability exercise to your routine this week, performed slowly enough to notice where your body compensates.
If you have been focusing purely on distance/power exercises, add one rotational deceleration or resistance exercise this week before adding any new power work.
Sketch a simple four-week outline for your own training, sequencing mobility work in week one before layering in strength and power in later weeks, rather than doing all exercise types at once.
reflectionQuestions: Which part of your swing do you (or a coach) consistently identify as a technical flaw — and could it actually be a physical limitation in disguise?
How does your current pre-round routine compare to a genuinely swing-specific warm-up?
Are you currently training for power without having first addressed your ability to safely decelerate and control that same force?

points: As an exercise manual rather than a controlled research study, the book's exercise selections are based on the authors' clinical and coaching experience rather than published, peer-reviewed efficacy trials specific to golf performance outcomes; readers should treat the program as expert-informed practice rather than clinically proven protocol.

The book assumes access to gym-style equipment and a baseline level of exercise literacy for many of its 72 exercises; it is less immediately usable for a complete beginner without some guidance on safe form, despite the step-by-step descriptions.

Golf swing biomechanics and the resulting injury patterns vary meaningfully by individual anatomy, swing style, and existing injury history; a generalized program, even a well-sequenced one, is not a substitute for individualized assessment by a qualified professional for anyone with an existing injury.

The book's second edition (used for this entry) updates and expands the first edition; readers should confirm which edition they own, since exercise selection and chapter structure changed between editions.
criticalTake.contextNote: The underlying biomechanical principles (kinetic chain sequencing, mobility-before-stability-before-power progression) are well-established in general sports science and have not meaningfully "aged" since publication, though specific exercise trends in strength and conditioning continue to evolve.

whoThisIsFor: Golfers experiencing inconsistency, lack of distance, or recurring physical discomfort who want to address the physical, rather than purely technical, side of their game, and golf coaches or fitness trainers looking for a structured reference.
whenToReadThis: Best used as an ongoing reference alongside an actual training program rather than read once and set aside — particularly useful at the start of a golf season or when recovering from a swing-related injury.

authorBio.name: Craig Davies and Vince DiSaia
authorBio.bio:
Dr. Craig Davies is a chiropractor and movement, body mechanics, and strength and conditioning coach who has worked with more than fifty professional golfers across tours including the PGA, Nationwide, European, Canadian, LPGA, and Futures Tours. He developed the Golf Exercise Specialist and Golf Performance Therapist certifications and has served as a keynote speaker at golf performance industry events.

Dr. Vince DiSaia is a strength and conditioning specialist and chiropractor specializing in fitness and therapy for elite golf performance, certified as a medical golf fitness professional through the Titleist Performance Institute. He has worked with amateur and touring professionals across multiple tours and co-founded a company producing instructional exercise programs for rehabilitation and strength training.

Together, the two authors bring a combined clinical and performance-coaching background to the book, aiming to translate high-level golf fitness practice, developed originally for touring professionals, into a structured resource usable by amateur golfers and fitness professionals working with golf clients.
